But having motion follows from being a mover."},"philosophy":{"insight":"If motion is inherent in the mover, the mover should always be moving. But movers also rest (exhibit non-motion). This creates a direct contradiction: the definition (\"mover\" entails motion) clashes with observed reality (movers can be still).","madhyamaka":"Garfield: this verse deepens the v.3 argument — if motion is intrinsic, non-motion becomes impossible for that entity, which is absurd. Kalupahana: the verse exposes the Sarvāstivādin difficulty of treating motion as a \"real\" dharma possessed by a \"real\" agent. Siderits/Katsura: the verse uses a reductio — accept inherent motion, then non-motion becomes inexplicable.","quantum":"Superposition Collapse / Measurement Problem: Before measurement, a qubit exists in superposition of |moving⟩ and |stationary⟩. Measurement collapses it to one definite state. You cannot say the particle \"inherently\" possesses motion if measurement can also find it stationary.","bridge":"Both show inherent properties create contradictions with observed variability. If motion were inherent, non-motion would be impossible — just as if a qubit \"inherently\" had spin-up, measuring spin-down would be impossible. The fact that both outcomes occur proves neither is inherent.","accessible":"If \"being funny\" were an inherent property of a comedian, they could never be serious. But comedians are serious all the time! So \"funny\" isn't inherent — it depends on context. Similarly, \"moving\" isn't inherent to a mover, because movers also rest.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, we say \"the car moves\" — perfectly functional. Ultimately, motion can't be an inherent property OF the mover — it's a relational, dependent event.","commonMisconception":"Not denying that things move. Denying that motion is a pre-existing inherent property waiting to be expressed. Motion is relational, not possessed."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Superposition Collapse / Measurement Problem","score":87,"strength":"High","explanation":"Inherent properties would preclude opposite measurement outcomes. So \"employed\" is a conditional state, not an inherent nature."},{"q":"How does superposition collapse parallel this exactly?","a":"A qubit in superposition α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ doesn't \"inherently have\" either value. Similarly, if a mover inherently had motion, non-motion would be impossible — but it occurs.","realLifeExample":"Flipping a coin can land heads or tails. Both outcomes prove neither is inherent — the result depends on the flip (context)."},{"q":"Is this argument a reductio ad absurdum?","a":"Yes. Nāgārjuna assumes the opponent's premise (motion is inherent in the mover) and derives a contradiction (non-motion would be impossible, but it occurs). Since the conclusion is absurd, the premise must be false.","realLifeExample":"Assume: \"All birds can fly.\" Observe: penguins are birds but can't fly. Conclusion: the assumption is wrong. That's a reductio — accepting the premise leads to contradiction with observed facts."},{"q":"Does this mean motion is an illusion?","a":"No! Motion is conventionally real — things genuinely move.
